title: World Cup games could face extended weather delays due to lack of FIFA cut-off point
content:
World Cup fixtures could face lengthy delays if they are interrupted by severe weather conditions as FIFA does not have a cut-off point in its regulations for calling a match off.

According to U.S. thunderstorm protocol, a fixture taking place at a stadium must be immediately suspended if lightning or electrical discharge is detected within an eight-mile radius of the venue.

The players are led off the pitch and must take shelter in their dressing room, while fans are evacuated to safe areas inside the venue.

Once a lightning strike has been detected within eight miles, then a 30-minute countdown clock begins.

And if this time passes without any further strikes, then the match can resume. However, if there is another lightning strike during that 30-minute window, then the clock is reset to zero, and it will continue to be reset until 30 minutes pass without a detected strike.

Although FIFA is not responsible for U.S. thunderstorm protocol, nor can they override it, this could lead to World Cup fixtures being delayed for hours.

FIFA does not have a specific regulation that stipulates how long a delay has to last before a match is eventually called off, although they will assess it on a case by case basis. Postponing a game would also create scheduling issues.

Last month, world football’s governing body released a detailed statement addressing the impact adverse weather conditions may have on the tournament.

“FIFA’s emergency preparedness team meets regularly with national meteorological and emergency management authorities in the United States, Canada and Mexico, as well as with partners across all 16 Host Cities,” the statement read.

“A comprehensive, tournament-wide preparedness exercise focusing on severe weather scenarios has further strengthened cross-agency coordination and operational readiness.

“Stadiums are required to maintain robust risk management and evacuation procedures, including lightning and severe weather protocols aligned with local legislation and international best practice.”

The statement goes on to add that FIFA will be monitoring “conditions in real time” by “integrating Wet Bulb Globe Temperature and Heat Index surveillance”, noting that they would be “ready to apply established contingency protocols should extreme weather events occur”.

During last summer’s Club World Cup, which was hosted in the United States, a number of games were delayed due to extreme conditions. Chelsea’s fixture against Benfica in Charlotte lasted a staggering four hours and 38 minutes after it was interrupted by what FIFA described as “severe weather in the area”.

The delay lasted around two hours and Enzo Maresca, then Chelsea’s head coach, described the situation as a “joke”.
